articles.title_orig: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
articles.title_zh: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market.
The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half.
GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models.
"All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan.
The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers.
"Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation.
GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal.
The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage.
GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities .
Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses.
He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad.
"There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise."
GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines.
The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems.
That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features.
The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs.
GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact.
GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them.
"We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them."
GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development.
The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed.
"This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release.
GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development.
The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype.
Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028.
Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar.
"In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools."
The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers.
GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand.
The OnStar AI assistant is expected to launch in the coming months on the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq EV through an over-the-air update before expanding to other models.
GM currently uses Google's Gemini for its in-vehicle AI assistant. The company told CNBC earlier this year that the GM-developed AI will be more integrated with the vehicle.
The goal for OnStar AI, which will be available through a subscription, is to help customers be productive while in the car, especially if the vehicle has self-driving capabilities that don't require the driver or passengers to monitor the system.
GM on Wednesday also reiterated its plans to launch eyes-off highway driving in 2028. The automaker said a year ago that it wanted to launch that technology. It's been five years since Barra said she expected the automaker to offer personal autonomous vehicles this decade.
"Our vision is that eventually every vehicle should drive itself or its occupants anywhere, and we're investing across the self-driving stack to make that real," Anderson said.

articles.content_orig:

The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation .
PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites . It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.
The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.
Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.
So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.
Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open-source source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post . Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.
Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help.
Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)
OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.
In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.
Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia spends billions on its military. Why can't it stop deadly attacks by Iran's Houthi allies?
articles.content_orig:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom, with missiles hitting energy infrastructure and civilian airports , killing at least 20 people.
The Iranian proxy group has struck the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, and is fighting Saudi-backed government forces for control of Yemen's coastline on the Red Sea, a vital waterway for global energy supplies. The fighting has put further upward pressure on oil and gas prices as Iran and the U.S. fight over the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels. The kingdom's opaque government releases regular statements about Houthi ballistic missiles and drones being intercepted, including five it said were destroyed Wednesday.
But many have got through, including an Oct. 10 strike that killed 13 people at Riyadh's King Khalid Airport, including a U.S. citizen.
"No country can ever have a 100% interception rating, that just doesn't really exist," Elizabeth Dent, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told CBS News, but that "was a hell of a one to miss."
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East , including Israel.
So why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage?
Saudi Arabia is vast and, analysts say, geographically vulnerable.
Its east, home to the kingdom's oil fields, is bordered by the Persian Gulf —   all that separates Saudi Arabia from longtime foe Iran. Early in the war, Iran launched strikes targeting bases used by the U.S. in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for U.S. attacks.
To the north, across Saudi Arabia's long border with Iraq, are Iran-backed militia groups that the Saudis —   along with the U.S. — struck in July in response to dozens of attempted drone attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure and on U.S. installations in the region.
To the south, Saudi Arabia shares a more-than-800-mile border with Yemen. A vast portion of the war-wracked nation is controlled by the Houthis. To Saudi Arabia's west, the Houthis have also been battling for control of the Red Sea's vital shipping lanes.
"Over the last eight months, they have been facing threats from every direction," said Dent.
"There is a lot of critical infrastructure: multiple airports, many pipelines, as well as extensive oil production and export infrastructure, military bases, government buildings, royal palaces, and so on," said Thomas Juneau, associate fellow at the Chatham House think tank's Middle East and North Africa Program. "It is simply extremely difficult to provide air defenses for all these sites over such a large area."
"If the Houthis are able to hit Saudi infrastructure with only a minority of their attempted drone or missile attacks, it counts as a success for them and an embarrassment and a loss for Saudi Arabia," Juneau told CBS News.
Neither Saudi nor Houthi authorities responded to CBS News' request for comment on this story.
The ongoing wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have caused a global supply shortage of the interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles and other weapons, including the U.S.-made Patriot system used by Saudi Arabia and other American allies.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about Ukraine's longstanding request for Patriot interceptors, said Tuesday that "every other country in the world" also wants them.
"I also talked to Saudi Arabia today. They'd like interceptors. Israel would like interceptors. We would like interceptors. Every country in the world would like interceptors," Rubio said, calling it "probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field."
"Demand coming from the international [market] is stronger than ever," Tim Cahill, president of missiles and fire control at Lockheed Martin, the world's biggest weapons manufacturer and maker of the Patriot interceptors, told CBS News last week when asked about the short supply.
Saudi Arabia is secretive about its weapons systems and stockpiles, but CBS News reported in March that Gulf countries were seeking emergency resupplies of interceptors , while the Wall Street Journal and Associated Press have reported that the kingdom has sought air defense systems from Japan, South Korea, France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.
Patriot interceptors are expensive, costing as much as $4 million per unit .
"If there's fear over utilizing or drawing down your resources," said Dent, "are you more reticent to pull the trigger?"
Saudi Arabia has purchased 730 Patriot interceptors from Washington since 2020, according to U.S. military data , but even if it does have enough, the pricey missiles aren't ideal for combating everything in the Houthi arsenal.
Patriots were designed to intercept ballistic missiles, and the Houthis have launched those at Saudi Arabia. But the rebels also have an array of relatively cheap drones, including weapons supplied by Iran, and locally made copies of Iranian attack drones .
These inexpensive weapons have been a key element in the Houthis' tactics, analysts say.
They can be launched in swarms, Allison Minor, a senior fellow in the Middle East Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CBS News.
The Houthis "combine an overwhelming number of relatively cheap systems, namely drones, to distract and disrupt and exhaust, and then amid that, also weave in these more catastrophic missile attacks," she said.
The Saudis' multi-layered air defense system is sophisticated, but Houthi drones and cruise missiles can change their trajectory, making them harder to track, said Dent, "so if one aspect of that layered defense system breaks down, it can create a gap in coverage, like what may have occurred for the airport attack."
"This is a whole new ballgame," said Dent. "It's a tactic that requires some adjustments."
One possible solution could be Ukrainian-developed drone interceptors, which cost in the thousands of dollars to manufacture and are produced in the tens of thousands annually, unlike Patriots, which are produced in the hundreds .
Saudi Arabia and some of its neighbors have already made deals with Ukraine to acquire such systems, but Dent said they won't be a quick fix as "a lot of what the Ukrainians have been implementing is very hands-on."
The systems require skilled operators, in other words, and they require training.
Another issue is the Saudi personnel available to receive that training. Analysts do not rate the kingdom's military among the world's best, despite its huge defense budget.
Saudi Arabia's armed forces have a reputation for being "structured and run according to the interests of its royal leadership, with an emphasis on regime security," said CBS News national security analyst Aaron MacLean.
"You can spend all the money you want on your military and your missile defenses, but you also have to have a culture of readiness and excellence among the troops responsible," he said.
"If that's lacking, again, the problem is inherently a hard one: fighting intelligent people who really are trying to kill you and are willing to be quite creative in their pursuit of that goal," he said. "Some shots are going to get through."
Faced with Houthi successes and dwindling Patriots, the Saudis have been "aggressively seeking out air defense support from a variety of partners," said Minor, at CSIS.
The kingdom has invoked a mutual defense pact signed last year with Pakistan and Turkey, under which an attack on one country is considered an attack on all three, much like the NATO alliance's Article 5 . Pakistan has already confirmed a troop deployment to the kingdom, and Turkey is also working toward sending forces .

A recent report by Bloomberg details a canceled game in the Sims franchise from EA. In a letter to staff, EA announced the cancellation of “Project Lotus,” which was in development for the Sims series. Instead, the company plans to focus on a different initiative called “Project Evergreen.” Additionally, the development of another game, Skate, will continue, but the team working on it will be downsized.

Additionally, their online shooter Apex Legends, as well as upcoming action-adventure games such as the next installment in the Star Wars Jedi series and the Iron Man game from Motive, will not be affected. The Battlefield series will also continue, and Respawn and DICE appear to be collaborating on a new project as well.

articles.title_zh: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.content_orig:
Patients whose eye scans were read by an AI programme got results in 30 seconds, compared to facing an average waiting time of 23 days for results from a doctor, a study in Tanzania has shown.
Millions of people around the world have diabetic retinopathy, a condition where high blood sugar levels damage the tiny blood vessels in the retina.
It can lead to irreversible blindness if left untreated. Around a third of the 23 million people with diabetes in Africa have the complication.
In its early stages, diabetic retinopathy can have no symptoms, and the World Health Organization recommends that people living with diabetes undergo regular screening to check their eye health, so that they can be treated if necessary.
For the new study, published in the Lancet Global Health , researchers randomly assigned over 2,000 patients with diabetes visiting clinics in Tanzania’s Kilimanjaro and Arusha regions to either receive usual screening care, or to have a new type of AI-assisted screening.
Two fifths of the participants had changes in their eyes that needed referral to specialist care. In the half screened using AI, 36 per cent attended the central ophthalmology clinic within eight weeks, compared to 18 per cent in the standard care group.
Most of the people working in the regions where the study was based are farmers, said Dr Justus Rwiza of the Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre, co-author on the paper. “They depend on vision.”
The economic effects of blindness are felt by the whole family, he said, recalling how the daughter of one patient “had to stop schooling to help the mother”.
In both arms of the trial, people attending local health clinics had photographs taken of the back of their eyes.
Under usual care, the photographs were sent to specialists to be assessed at a later date, and the patient received a phone call or text message to be told if they needed to attend a clinic for follow-up. The average time between scan and results was 23 days.
In the other half of the trial, AI was used to read the eye images immediately, with results “within 30 seconds”. Patients were told if they needed a referral there and then.
Dr Charles Cleland, ophthalmologist and clinical research fellow at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said the immediate AI diagnosis enabled patients to better understand the significance of their screening results via “face-to-face counselling at the point of screening, giving people the opportunity to ask questions, understand treatment options and feel supported in their care”.
The number of people living with diabetes in Tanzania is projected to rise from two million to seven million by 2050.
Tanzania has a shortage of trained eye specialists, and the results suggest AI could help ease some of the pressure on that workforce, Cleland added, in order to “improve access to specialist care and help prevent irreversible sight loss”.
The Tanzanian government now plans to roll out the AI-assisted screening more widely.

Helen Haines, the Australian MP struck by a car outside her constituency office in an alleged attack on Monday, has had her second leg amputated, her husband has announced.
Addressing the media on Wednesday afternoon, Phil Haines said: “Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family.”
Surgeons on Monday had amputated Ms Haines’ left leg on Monday night after she was airlifted to hospital. The 65-year-old was struck twice by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office in Wangaratta in Victoria .
A suspect identified as Brendan Nugent, 43 , faces three charges over the alleged attack on the Independent MP, as police consider bringing additional charges against him. He remained silent during his first court appearance earlier on Wednesday.
Providing an update to the media on behalf of their family, Mr Haines said his wife’s road to “recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover. And that is what we hope for.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person, incredibly supportive of all around her; her family, her community, anybody she comes across and her mind.
“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
He said that the couple will celebrate their 40th anniversary in November and, in the last four months, have welcomed four grandchildren.
Thanking the public for the support that has been extended to the family, Mr Haines paid special tribute to first responders at the scene of the alleged attack on Monday, including police, paramedics and the members of the community.
“One thing I’ve learned in the last two days, reinforced by many people, is to take things day by day. I know it’s a cliche, but it’s a cliche for a very good reason.
“So I thank you all for being here. I thank you for listening. And please keep sending Helen your love and our family as well.”
Australia’s governor-general Sam Mostyn said she was “touched” to be invited by Mr Haines to attend the press conference, and also expressed gratitude towards the first responders.
She reiterated that Ms Haines’ recovery would be taken “day by day” after what she described as Monday’s “violent attack”.
She called on Australians to “do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack” and to “not descend into violence and chaos and division”.
The incident has shocked Australia , a country where political violence is rare and politicians have always been accessible to the public. Most MPs and even senior ministers go about their work and personal lives without being accompanied by security teams.
Prime minister Anthony Albanese, who characterised the attack as deliberate, called for a calming of political rhetoric in the wake of the incident, and thanked bystanders for intervening . He also spoke with local barber Ricky Jefferies, who helped detain the suspect .

SpaceX will soon notch a huge spaceflight milestone, if all goes according to plan.
The company will try to catch both stages of its Starship megarocket during the vehicle's next test flight, which is targeted for next month, founder and CEO Elon Musk announced during SpaceX's quarter 3 (Q3) earnings call today (Oct. 20).
If SpaceX succeeds, this "will be the first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered," Musk said. "The only way that we can extend consciousness beyond Earth on a sustained basis is with a fully reusable orbital launch vehicle. So this is, I think, a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization and consciousness."
Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall when fully stacked.
As Musk noted, both of its stages — the Super Heavy booster and Ship spacecraft — are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX thinks will make Mars settlement and other grand exploration feats economically feasible.
Starship's recovery strategy is different than that for SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets, which are partially reusable. (The latter two rockets have expendable upper stages). Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy boosters come back to Earth on landing pads near the launch site or on ships at sea downrange. Super Heavy and Ship, however, will steer themselves directly back to their launch tower, which will capture each vehicle with its "chopstick" arms.
This will allow SpaceX to inspect, refurbish and refly Starship at an accelerated rate, which is a priority for the company: Musk has said he envisions launching Starship more than 10,000 times per year by 2030.
Starship has conducted 14 test flights to date, and SpaceX has pulled off chopstick catches with Super Heavy on three of them. The company has not yet tried to catch Ship, which is a more difficult proposition, as the upper stage travels higher, farther and faster than the booster does.
Still, Musk is confident that SpaceX will pull off a Ship catch on the first try. (He did not give a specific target date for Flight 15, saying only that it was expected next month.)
"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," he said. "And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year, and and then accelerating next year."
Success would mean back-to-back Starship flights with huge milestones. On Flight 14, which occurred on Sept. 28, Ship reached orbit for the first time ever . It also deployed 26 of SpaceX's Starlink Version 3 satellites — the first 26 members of a next-gen broadband constellation in low Earth orbit that will eventually consist of about 100,000 spacecraft .
The Starship Flight 15 preview was something of an aside during today's call. The event primarily served to announce SpaceX's financial performance during Q3, the three-month stretch that ended on Sept. 30.
And that performance was strong, company representatives said. SpaceX recorded revenues of $14.6 billion during Q3, an increase of 161% from the $5.6 billion earned during Q3 of 2025. The company had a net income of $4.4 billion during Q3, $5.5 billion better than the result from the same stretch last year, when SpaceX lost $1.1 billion.
Just $1.8 billion of 2026 Q3 revenue came from SpaceX's launch division. The vast majority was generated by two other segments — connectivity (services provided by its Starlink megaconstellation) and artificial intelligence (or, as the Trump administration has recently rebranded it, "superintelligence").
SpaceX thinks these latter two segments will continue to boom. That's why it's building the infrastructure to support thousands of Starship launches per year — to loft lots of Starlink satellites and AI data centers to Earth orbit. And the company believes that it's positioned to really start raking in the cash, starting as soon as next year.
"In a nutshell, what this implies for SpaceX annual recurring revenue by the end of '27 is somewhere between 500 billion [dollars] and a trillion," Musk said.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.content_orig:
The letter asks Google CEO Sundar Pichai to respond by Nov. 2 on what the company knows about AI's effect on students
Kevin Carter / Getty Images
Sens. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, sent a letter to Google $GOOGL CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect the mental health of kids and their growth as learners, according to The Wall Street Journal .
The senators wrote that they have "grave concern" that Google 's "aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation." They set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to reply.
The letter asks Pichai how much Google understands about the ways its AI tools might harm children, why AI features were made the default setting on school devices, which worries districts, teachers and parents have voiced about students leaning on AI academically and emotionally, and which promotions Google has used to broaden the use of AI in schools.
" Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price," the senators wrote, according to The Wall Street Journal. "We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples' best interest."
The letter cites a September Wall Street Journal investigation. Drawing on more than 60 conversations with educators, school officials, parents, students and clinicians, the investigation found that many students have grown emotionally and academically reliant on Google 's AI tools, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Journal also spoke with current and former Google staff and examined the company's research papers, which showed that Google 's own researchers have cautioned that the technology can carry heightened risks for children and may cause cognitive and emotional harm, according to The Wall Street Journal.
A Google spokesperson pointed The Wall Street Journal to a statement the company issued previously, which read “teachers around the world use our technology every day because it solves real classroom challenges and helps improve learning outcomes.” The statement said Google develops its products by working alongside educators and leaves teachers and administrators in charge of how they are used. Google has said it promotes critical thinking and built safeguards aimed at users younger than 18, among them steps meant to head off emotional dependence, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Slipping test scores have driven a backlash against classroom screen time among people of all political stripes, according to The Wall Street Journal. Parent anger has prompted districts such as New York City and Los Angeles to suspend AI use by students in their classrooms through moratoriums, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Chromebooks make up roughly 59% of the devices in U.S. schools, according to Crypto Briefing . By early October, Google had extended access to its Gemini student hub to every K-12 user on Google Workspace for Education, according to Crypto Briefing.
In a July report, Common Sense Media found that the AI tools built into Google Search, such as AI Overview and AI Mode, present an “unacceptable risk” to kids, according to Crypto Briefing. A Senate HELP subcommittee convened on Oct. 9 to examine how AI is affecting K-12 education, according to Crypto Briefing.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump Urges UK to Go 'Full Blast' on North Sea Gas After Scottish Gas Drilling Approval
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump Urges UK to Go 'Full Blast' on North Sea Gas After Scottish Gas Drilling Approval
articles.content_orig:
By JAMES TAPSFIELD, UK POLITICAL EDITOR and TOM LAWRENCE, NEWS REPORTER
Published: 02:03 EDT, 21 October 2026 | Updated: 11:57 EDT, 21 October 2026
Andy Burnham was urged to go further in opening up North Sea drilling today after the Jackdaw gas project finally received approval.
The PM defended the decision in the Commons this lunchtime despite a backlash from the Labour Left, Greens and environmental groups.
But Kemi Badenoch insisted that now he had accepted that the move bolsters 'energy security' he should allow more gas and oil licences.
The message was echoed by Donald Trump , who took to Truth Social to praise 'great news' and said the UK should go 'full blast'.
'The UK has started drilling in the North Sea, one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of OIL in the World. They should go FULL BLAST!!! This will make the UK very wealthy again,' the president said.
The Jackdaw project was approved by the previous Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed after a legal challenge by Greenpeace, leaving Labour ministers to decide whether drilling should go ahead.
Downing Street insists a 2024 manifesto pledge against new developments in the North Sea does not apply, as the site was already earmarked.
It is expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6 per cent at its peak, safeguard hundreds of jobs and provide an estimated £2.9billion economic boost.
Tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas will also be funnelled into a new energy wealth fund, backed with an initial £2billion, which will be used to invest in renewable and low carbon projects.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh accepted this morning that the development would contribute towards climate change, and said it would not bring down gas prices.
But she stressed it is 'much better' to use domestically produced gas than import it.
The Cabinet minister also appeared to hint that a second project at Rosebank might not be greenlit, suggesting that oil was less relevant to domestic energy issues.
There are claims that some Labour MPs are staying quiet on Jackdaw in the hopes of winning the argument on Rosebank and other Net Zero debates.
At PMQs, Andy Burnham said he had asked the Chancellor and Net Zero Secretary to consider whether the levy - typically around 30p a day - could be removed
The message was echoed by Donald Trump, who took to Truth Social to praise 'great news' and said the UK should go 'full blast'
The Tories said ministers had 'wasted' two years 'faffing' over whether to go ahead
Kemi Badenoch welcomed the move to sign off the North Sea drilling scheme despite a backlash from the Labour Left and Greens
In the Commons, Mrs Badenoch said ministers had 'dithered' for two years over whether to go ahead, insisting if the decision had been taken earlier gas would be heating UK homes this winter.
She demanded Labour repeals its ban on all new oil and gas licences in the North Sea.
'We have the resources, the expertise and the people,' Mrs Badenoch said. 'What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions'.
Mrs Badenoch had mocked the lack of cheering from Labour MPs at the mention of the Jackdaw approval.
But Mr Burnham said the Tory government had 'messed up'. 'That's why there was the delay, because they didn't do the process properly,' he said. 'And we've made a pragmatic decision, Mr Speaker, that will allow us to do two things.
'Firstly, build a bridge to a renewable future because the resources that come in now from this decision will allow us to invest in renewables, bring forward clean energy and in this Parliament, substantially de-link gas and electricity prices so that we can bring bills down.
'It will also allow us, Mr Speaker, to do more to help people with bills. I can tell the House today that I have asked the Chancellor and the Energy Secretary (Miatta Fahnbulleh) to look at whether we can remove standing charges from gas bills and to report back to this House at the earliest opportunity.'
Ed Miliband - who was promoted from Net Zero Secretary to Foreign Secretary when Mr Burnham became PM in July, was not in the chamber for the weekly clashes today. He was rumoured to have been resisting the Jackdaw approval, although officials insisted he was busy with the Oman state visit.
Speaking in Aberdeen earlier, Ms Fahnbulleh said: 'The reality is, as we put billions into low carbon energy and we do make that transition, we're going to need gas.
'And, ultimately, if you have a choice between homegrown gas that is on our doorstep that I can make sure that there are conditions in terms of the emissions that come out of that production, or I'm importing that gas or oil from across the world – I think it is much better for us to have homegrown gas.
'It supports our energy security and, critically, it means we are securing jobs here in Aberdeen.'
Ms Fahnbulleh told BBC Radio Scotland of the looming Rosebank decision: 'Each project we have got to take on their own merits and I've got to look at them case by case in isolation.
'But they are two very difference projects.
'Jackdaw is producing gas that predominantly is used in the domestic market, Rosebank is a different proposition because it is oil that is exported.
'So I'll look at it against a series of tests and we'll make the judgment on that at the right point.
'But the decisions are very different and it's important that they remain separate.'
Mr Burnham added: 'At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help.
'We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050.
'But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come.
'That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea. We're also establishing a new Energy Wealth Fund to invest in renewable energy, support the green transition and help reduce energy bills over the long-term.
'Our approach will ensure we can boost our energy security, back British workers, ringfence future North Sea proceeds to speed up the green transition, hit our ambitious climate targets and – crucially – bring down bills.'
The PM could be particularly vulnerable on his Left flank, after successfully wooing back a chunk of support from the Greens in recent months.
Zack Polanski immediately seized on the news to accuse ministers of 'climate vandalism'.
'Today's decision by Labour is a betrayal of all of our futures, Labour has abandoned all credibility in the fight against climate change,' he said.
'The Energy Secretary has herself said it will make no difference to energy bills; the Health Secretary has admitted the summer heatwave added to pressure on the NHS, and the industry's own assessment is that it will create only 27 jobs.
'This is a victory for Shell over the people.'
Labour MP Alex Sobel, the head of the Left-wing Mainstream group that helped make Mr Burnham leader, told Politico: 'Jackdaw won't draw gas for many years. Won't make an impact on global prices and will give mixed messages in terms of investment in terms of both renewables and decarbonisation of home heating.'
Nadia Whittome posted on X: 'Approving the drilling of Jackdaw is the wrong decision on every front. It won't bring down bills, it creates barely any jobs, and it undermines our climate commitments.
'True energy security comes from rapidly expanding homegrown renewables, not continuing our reliance on volatile fossil fuels.
'The idea that we need more drilling to fund them is exactly what the fossil fuel lobby wants us to believe.'
Fellow Labour MP Apsana Begum said: 'The approval of Jackdaw will not lower our household energy bills, nor will it make us more resilient in the face of climate breakdown.
'It will however, further damage trust in democracy, as ''no new oil and gas'' was promised just 2 years ago.
'If the Government approve Rosebank too, this will only signal an end

articles.title_orig: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.title_zh: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.content_orig:
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.
In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.
Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.
The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.
A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.
The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.
K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.
On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.
In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.
In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.
Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.
The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.
In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”
In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.
“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

articles.title_orig: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
articles.title_zh: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
articles.content_orig:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".
"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.
The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.
She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.
"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.
The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".
He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".
Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.
"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.
He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".
Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."
Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.
But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully .
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.
The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.
In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined .
"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

articles.title_zh: Elon Musk says he’s staying in Memphis ‘night and day’ guiding data center buildout
articles.content_orig:
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Elon Musk said he is spending four days a week in Memphis to get the Colossus 2 supercomputer cluster online.
“I’ve been spending personally a lot of my time in Memphis, often four days a week, night and day, just getting the Memphis SuperCompute cluster or Colossus 2 online,” Musk, SpaceXAI founder and CEO, said on Tuesday’s SpaceX earnings call. “We’re tracking to be able to bring roughly 200,000 GB300s online per month for every month for the remainder of this year and continuing that pace next year.”
Musk’s Colossus supercomputer campus has grown over the last two years, adding a second, larger site in Memphis and relying on gas turbines across the state line in Southaven , Mississippi, to meet power demand.
That growth has drawn a federal lawsuit from the NAACP , which says the turbines ran for months without a required air permit .
The buildout has drawn years of pushback from South Memphis neighbors and environmental groups over air quality and water use.
This week, a federal judge rejected the Trump administration’s bid to throw out the NAACP’s Clean Air Act lawsuit over the turbines powering the site.

articles.title_orig: Websites taken down across Europe as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.title_zh: Websites taken down across Europe as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.content_orig:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X , Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are " temporarily down for maintenance " without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. They used state-of-the art AI, made by OpenAI, to find the flaws.
OpenAI said in a blog post it was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
According to the firms, they had gone undetected for more than a decade.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note .
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning .
"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.
"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".
The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in push to simplify operations, internal memo shows
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: EBay to lay off 9% of workforce in push to simplify operations, internal memo shows
articles.content_orig:
EBay will lay off about 9% of its workforce in a move to streamline its operations and focus on its fastest-growing areas, a company spokesperson confirmed to CNBC. The layoffs will affect approximately 1,000 employees.
"As we work to capture the significant opportunity ahead, this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities," the spokesperson said in a statement.
The company also said it will continue to hire in "priority areas aligned with our strategy." As of the end of 2025, eBay had roughly 12,300 employees.
Reuters first reported the news, citing a memo to staff from CEO Jamie Iannone that read in part, "Our strategy is working."
"Continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest," Iannone said in the memo, seen by Reuters.
This is the second round of layoffs for the online marketplace this year, following a 6% workforce reduction that affected about 800 employees, in February. The company has been steadily shrinking its headcount over recent years at the same time it's ramping up spending on artificial intelligence.
EBay also acquired the used clothing resale platform Depop — a brand with a strong customer base of Gen Z and millennial users — from Etsy earlier this year. The $1.4 billion deal was finalized in July .
Shares of eBay were up approximately 1% Wednesday morning.
— CNBC's Annie Palmer contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.title_zh: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.content_orig:
Earlier this month AMD senior vice president Jack Huynh told media in South Korea that FSR 4 was coming to more devices, including handhelds - and now that promise has been fulfilled.
Huynh today announced that FSR 4.1 was coming to five new platforms: Radeon RX 6000-series graphics cards; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo mini PCs and mobile workstations; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo Ryzen 9 laptops; Z2 Extreme and Z2A handhelds like ROG Xbox Ally devices; and Xbox Series X and Series S.
It's a welcome surprise to see AMD's latest generation upscaler on a huge range of extra devices - even though community modders have been working hard to port the technique to an even longer list of supported platforms.
FSR 4, previously known as Project Redstone, is AMD's first machine learning upscaler and offers a significant visual advantage over its earlier efforts at similar frame-rates - hence the interest in making it available on a wider range of PCs, handhelds and other devices. As well as upscaling and anti-aliasing, the tech also includes frame generation and ray reconstruction, giving it better feature parity with Nvidia's similar DLSS tech.
Huynh's announcement also states that FSR is coming to Vulkan, a graphics API that is the default choice for games that don't use (or want to offer an alternative to) DirectX 12. FSR 3 and earlier supported Vulkan, so it's good to see this limitation redressed - though it's not clear how quickly developers will be able to add FSR 4.1 support to their Vulkan games.
More APUs will get FSR 4.1 support in the future, Huynh claimed, and the announcement video also mentions that AMD's next-gen FSR Diamond will be supported on Xbox's Project Helix " family of devices ".
If you want to use FSR 4.1 on your PC (officially) for the first time, you'll need to install Adrenalin Edition version 26.10.1 . The graphics drivers also add support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Final Fantasy Resonance.

articles.title_orig: Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack but ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says
articles.title_zh: Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack but ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’, husband says
articles.content_orig:
Haines is in stable condition. Surgeons tried to save her right leg but both have now been amputated due to injuries
Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast
The independent MP Helen Haines has lost both legs but remains in a stable condition, two days after an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria.
Haines, the federal MP for Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.
Her husband, Phil Haines, provided an update on his wife’s condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital late on Wednesday afternoon.
Composed and clear, he said his wife had survived a “horrendous incident” and faced a long road to recovery.
“The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable,” he said.
“That is the most important thing for our family. And I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”
Phil Haines described his wife, 65, as a fighter. The pair have been married for nearly 40 years and have three children and two grandchildren. He became emotional for a moment at the end of the statement, reflecting on his wife’s strength.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover, and that is what we hope for,” he said.
“We are grateful at this stage that both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
Haines asked for donations to Save the Children as his wife recovers. A special appeal has been launched by the charity.
Police allege Monday’s attack was targeted, and have charged Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Nugent faced Wangaratta magistrates court earlier on Wednesday.
Phil Haines was joined by the governor general, Sam Mostyn. Mostyn said she had relayed news of the incident to King Charles and praised Helen Haines’s work as a local representative, including her commitment to improving the standards of public discourse in Australia.
“This violent attack on a much loved and respected sitting member of our federal parliament must be a moment for us to pause and to choose to be better,” she said.
“We’ve got to hope that that beautiful heart, that beautiful mind will be strengthened every day by our support and our commitment to be more like Helen as part of this great democracy.”
Anthony Albanese and politicians from across federal parliament have expressed shock and anger at the alleged attack on Haines.
The incident has sparked calls for changes to politicians’ safety, with security services including the Australian federal police and Asio briefing MPs on the current landscape on Wednesday.
Speaking at a vigil in Wodonga on Wednesday evening, Cathy McGowan, who held the seat of Indi before Haines, paid tribute to her friend.
“There is another level of grief, different and deeper from the actual violence, from the sorrow, the shame and the hurt,” she said.
“It’s about Helen in her role as our elected representative. In attacking her, we intuit that this is an attack on our political system, on our democracy, and especially so for all the supporters who did the democracy work getting Helen elected.”
McGowan called for the upcoming Victorian state election campaign to be conducted in a positive and constructive way. Voters go to the polls next month.
The community could not let violence win, McGowan implored.
“That we ensure the legacy of this attack on Helen will be a stronger, more vibrant and effective democracy, and from a personal perspective, all candidates and especially women, know they can run for office and be safe.”

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo adding Apple Pencil support next week with iOS 27.2
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo adding Apple Pencil support next week with iOS 27.2
articles.content_orig:
If you open your new iPhone Duo on Friday then grab your Apple Pencil and start sketching, don't be surprised that it won't work. Apple's first foldable will be able to use a stylus, but not at launch. Still, that might change sooner than you realize.
No matter when the feature shows up, it's the answer to a request users have made for years.
iPhone and iPad can be used entirely with a fingertip, but Apple Pencil offers an option for those who want more precise input for handwritten notes, sketches, document annotations and even digital painting.
The initial version of the stylus launched in 2015, but it and successive versions support only iPad… until now. The upcoming iPhone Duo is the first iOS handset that can use the stylus.
"iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil with USB-C, allowing users to take notes, sketch, or mark up documents on either display," Apple promised on the day it announced the foldable.
iPhone users have asked Apple to bring Apple Pencil support to its smartphones for years, particularly as iPhone displays have grown larger. That's especially true of the 7.6-inch display in the Duo — that's 40% more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max.
When the iPhone Duo was first announced, all Cupertino would say about the timing of Apple Pencil support was "later this year." Reviews of the handset published on Wednesday considerably narrowed the window.
Engadget said the necessary support arrives "later this month" in its review , and Cnet used the exact same phrase .
See also: First iPhone Duo reviews call Apple's foldable impressive but not perfect
They didn't get more specific, but Creative Strategies analyst Max Weinbach said Wednesday that Apple Pencil support will be in iOS 27.2, which will almost certainly reach iPhones around the world on October 26 .
The iPhone Duo will work with Apple Pencil (USB-C). It will not support Apple Pencil Pro, as that version of the stylus requires a wireless charging port to be built into the device — a port the Duo does not have.
Still, while the pricey Pro version boasts additional features, the USB-C version costs considerably less. And it offers precise input, tilt sensitivity and low latency, making it useful for drawing, handwriting and annotating documents on the iPhone Duo display.
As Engadget put it, "The textured surface on its main panel should make drawing or taking notes with an Apple Pencil feel great."

articles.title_orig: NY congressional nominee Brad Lander says he was detained by the IDF in the West Bank
articles.title_zh: NY congressional nominee Brad Lander says he was detained by the IDF in the West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Lefty congressional nominee Brad Lander claimed Wednesday he was “detained” by the Israeli Defense Forces while working on an olive harvest in the West Bank.
Lander, the former Big Apple Comptroller who is running for Congress in the Nov. 3 election, posted a picture of himself glaring at the camera while onboard a bus with others who were on their phones and didn’t seem fazed.
“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis & volunteers,” Lander posted on X. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim in the West Bank.”
It is unclear if Lander, who is vying for New York’s 10th Congressional District seat, was doing anything else besides olive harvesting.
“The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know,” he added.
Lander had bested outgoing Rep. Dan Goldman (D-NY) in their June primary, mounting a challenge against him from the left. Lander, who is Jewish, has been an outspoken critic of Israel.
During his primary against Goldman and his unsuccessful run for mayor last year, Lander made Israel a top issue.
The Dem candidate has opposed unconditional military aid to the Jewish state and accused it of carrying out a genocide in the Gaza Strip after the bloody Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.
“I think — with deep sadness — that Israel’s conduct in Gaza meets the definition of genocide. But even if you don’t, it’s profoundly inconsistent with the Jewish value that every one of those Palestinian kids were created in the image of God, just like ours,” he posted on X in June.
Lander also contended that “Israel can’t be a genuine democracy while it’s occupying the West Bank & Gaza.”
Rabbis for Human Rights, an Israeli human rights group, corroborated Lander’s claim about being detained and said 90 other volunteers were held by the IDF as well, while harvesting olives in Nahalin, outside Bethlehem.
Authorities designated the area they were working in as a military zone closed for a full day, according to the group.
Officials then checked the group for identification, despite the group’s leaders offering to leave voluntarily, according to Rabbis for Human Rights’ version of events.
“We came to accompany farmers to land they have not been able to reach in three years, and after two hours of quiet harvesting, large forces arrived and closed the area,” Acting executive director for Rabbis for Human Rights, Anton Goodman, said in a statement.
“No one could have known about this order in advance. Instead of protecting people working their own land, the army is removing them from it, and detaining those who came to stand beside them.”
Lander previously described his venture to the West Bank as a mission to help Palestinians with their harvest and to put the spotlight on conditions there.
Other lefty pols have had similar run-ins with Israeli authorities. In July, for example, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said he and his group were detained by the Israelis for over an hour while in the Palestinian village of Khirbet Zanuta during a tour.

articles.title_orig: After A Year Of Layoffs, Disney Finds $180 Million For Recruits From Bankrupt Character.AI
articles.title_zh: After A Year Of Layoffs, Disney Finds $180 Million For Recruits From Bankrupt Character.AI
articles.content_orig:
Sign up to get our news digest — delivered directly to your inbox twice a week.
Disney has spent much of 2026 cutting jobs and announcing restrictions on employee benefits, with the reductions continuing under new CEO Josh D’Amaro. Now, it plans to spend roughly $180 million over three years to compensate and retain 66 recruits from the recently bankrupt, highly controversial chatbot startup Character.AI.
According to Business Insider , citing bankruptcy filings, the hiring follows September layoffs that included technology workers. The recruits are following former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand, whom Disney recently appointed its first company-wide chief technology officer. The group crossing over constitutes most of Character.AI’s approximately 86-person workforce at September’s end.
As we reported last week , Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 protection on October 12, ten days after Anand officially joined Disney. Disney separately offered $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license to certain intellectual property and certain company claims, subject to the bankruptcy sale process.
The spending adds another revealing chapter to Disney’s year of restructuring and continued efforts to get ahead in the AI race. The company eliminated jobs in January, approximately 1,000 more in April, and hundreds in July, including roughly 150 at Pixar .
In September, Disney’s top lawyer warned employees that his department would shrink substantially as the company considered automation, outside providers, and outsourcing. Beginning in 2027, Disney will also restrict spousal health coverage when spouses can obtain insurance through their own employers, even if those plans offer worse benefits.
These decisions come alongside substantial profits and shareholder payouts. Disney reported $5.6 billion in fiscal third-quarter segment operating income, up 21%, and raised its fiscal-year share-buyback target to at least $9 billion.
Big picture, the layoffs, benefit restrictions, buybacks, and AI hiring reveal consistent spending priorities. Disney is willing to commit substantial sums to AI expertise (remember its proposed $1 billion investment in OpenAI, announced alongside a Sora licensing deal that collapsed just over three months later, before any money changed hands?) and shareholder returns, while asking its existing workforce to absorb repeated cuts.

articles.content_orig:
European leaders are talking a big game on China, but will avoid a full-blown trade war due to internal division and fear of retaliation: analysts
The European Union is likely to avoid a full-blown trade confrontation with China due to internal divisions in the bloc and fear of retaliation, according to a prominent research firm.
But the bloc would “continue to pull its punches” in any confrontation with Beijing due to a lack of consensus among and within Europe’s member states, the London-based Capital Economics said at an event in Hong Kong on Wednesday.
The EU also had “concerns over retaliation” if it stepped up trade tensions with China, the research firm said, and held “lingering hopes to save the rules-based global trading system” that had helped Europe in the past.

articles.content_orig:
North Korea has told its border troops to take “prompt ​and resolute action” if South Korean forces threaten their safety, state media ​said on Wednesday, raising the risk of a clash along the ⁠heavily armed frontier.
The report came a day after Seoul pledged to punish “resolutely” any ​further provocation by Pyongyang if North Korea acted on threats to strengthen its military ​posture along the border.
North Korean Army Marshal Pak Jong Chon inspected fortifications on the border with South Korea on Tuesday, accompanied by Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong ​Un, KCNA reported.
Kim Yo Jong said new firepower units had “taken their firing positions” at ​the border, KCNA reported.
Tensions between North and South Korea have risen since Pyongyang began fortifying its ‌border ⁠in April 2024. The two countries are separated by the Demilitarized Zone that was established when the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.
Seoul says Pyongyang has sent up to 7,000 workers to the border this year, with about 50 ​crossings of the ​Military Demarcation Line, ⁠which bisects the DMZ, to South Korea’s side of the border.
These North Korean brothers spent 10 years planning their escape. Months after reaching freedom, everything changed
On Wednesday, North Korea rejected Seoul’s allegations, with Pak dismissing ​the claim as an “absurd assertion” designed to shift blame, KCNA reported.
The ​North Korean ⁠army knew where the border lay “better than any others” and was only doing what it should within its own territory, Pak said, urging soldiers to turn the border ⁠into an “impregnable ​fortress.”
South Korea said North Korean mines caused ​a border blast last month that seriously wounded two of its soldiers, and called on Pyongyang to suspend the ​fortification work.
